old_title: Woolly hats, battered bodies and big TV numbers mark rugby union's new festival finale
new_title: Woolly hats, battered bodies and big TV numbers mark rugby union's new festival finale
old_text:
It would be a stretch to describe the Nations Championship finals weekend as the "Glastonbury of Rugby" quite yet. Cher will certainly need to wrap up warm if she is planning to make a cameo appearance; with forecast temperatures of 3C, plenty more thermal vests and woolly hats will be in evidence than at Worthy Farm in June.
There will also be significant gaps in the Allianz Stadium moshpit when Italy and Fiji and Ireland and Australia kick off the three-day finals extravaganza beneath the Friday night lights. Even the organisers concede that Friday has been "a challenge" in terms of ticket sales and that's without factoring in rush-hour traffic and public transport disruption.
But, whisper it, Test rugby's newest vehicle has been appealing to viewers sitting comfortably at home. The organisers say the tournament is set to attract a total broadcast audience in excess of 100 million people, comparable to the 118 million fans in core markets who tuned in to this year's Six Nations. The Nations Championship will clearly have spanned many more games - 42 compared to 15 - but the hope is that ITV will have seen enough to renew for future tournaments.
Stadium attendances are also said to be up by 4% compared to previous November international windows, although punchy ticket prices this weekend seem to have deterred plenty with Christmas around the corner. The stadium will not be filled to capacity on either Saturday or Sunday and, as Andy Farrell, Ireland's head coach points out, it is not as simple as scheduling a game and expecting tens of thousands of green-shirted fans to drop everything. "Nobody knew until last weekend when we'd be playing," said Farrell. "The Irish can't buy flights over here because they're £1,000 so that doesn't work really."
There is also the small matter of player welfare; on top of the summer travel travails of some northern teams can now be added some visibly shattered southern bodies. "I can only imagine how the southern hemisphere boys are feeling now at the back end of their season," agrees Scotland's captain Sione Tuipulotu, himself now sidelined with a minor knee problem.
On the flipside, Tuipulotu and others have enjoyed the amended format in other ways. Scotland, for example, have been to South Africa and Argentina and hosted New Zealand and Australia inside five months. "I've loved it," says Tuipulotu, who should be back fit early next month. "Scottish teams don't normally get those summer fixtures."
Even New Zealand's Dave Rennie, whose side are crawling to the end of a year in which they will have played 13 of their 17 games (including provincial tour matches in South Africa) away from home, likes the change. "I like the concept. The interesting thing is you've got the northern hemisphere teams coming down to us at the end of their year and vice versa when we come up here. I just think our [Nations Championship] year is a little bit different to what it will be in two years' time when it is on again."
England's Steve Borthwick, for his part, is also upbeat ahead of this weekend's rematch with the All Blacks. "There's jeopardy in it, you start thinking about things which you weren't thinking of previously in the autumn. I would suggest that is a real positive aspect." Farrell, meanwhile, shares Rennie's view that 2028 should be less stressful for all involved. "This is a little bit different because the World Cup is next year. People are always going to have one eye on that. I think everyone's still trying to figure it out but it's certainly interesting. Let's see how this weekend goes."
South Africa's captain, Siya Kolisi, always someone with an eye on the bigger picture, is another fan regardless of whether his team edge out France in Sunday's grand final. "I think it's giving [the November Tests] more drive and more fans are excited about it. We've enjoyed it certainly as a team and I'm sure the other guys have all enjoyed it. Hopefully it continues."
More attention-grabbing games this weekend would further cement the concept. The venue for the 2028 edition will not be confirmed until the spring and it would not be a massive surprise if Paris or other French cities emerge as strong contenders. There remains a vision, too, for future promotion/relegation playoffs for each hemisphere; not every union fancies it but to allow the world's top dozen sides to remain unchallenged for ever would be a catastrophic look for the game's global profile.
That is not to say aspects of future editions cannot be finessed. The north-south trophy for the winning hemisphere was on precisely nobody's lips on Wednesday evening when all the head coaches - bar South Africa - were all speaking simultaneously in the Spirit of Rugby suite in Twickenham, temporarily transformed into an oval-shaped Tower of Babel. A Glastonbury festival vibe deep in a European winter might also be more practicable over a two-day weekend, or at least at a venue where large numbers of fans can party inside in the warm.
This weekend, regardless, already means different things to different people. Kolisi, as you would expect, is purely focused on winning yet another trophy for South Africa. "Everything that happened before that final game doesn't matter. It's all about whether you can rock up on the day and play to the best of your ability. And that's what we want to do."
One or two of rugby's other modern-day rock stars, though, sense the chance to let their hair down. "I love how we're all playing in London this week," says Tuipulotu. "There's a lot of rugby boys in one city ... I think there'll be few beers drunk after the game. Hopefully we can get through the weekend drama free."
But how do Scotland, who face Argentina on Sunday, feel about merely being an aperitif ahead of the grand final between the Springboks and France? "I'm not too sure," shrugs Tuipulotu. "But if you're coming for both games you've got five hours to drink as much beer as you can." Both on and off the field a lively weekend awaits.
